Burns

Small human trials report faster re-epithelialization or wound closure with selected PBM protocols for second-degree and donor-site burns. Results do not establish effects across all burn types or on long-term scarring and function.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small human trials report faster re-epithelialization or wound closure with selected PBM protocols for second-degree and donor-site burns. Results do not establish effects across all burn types or on long-term scarring and function.

Summary of the Evidence

The source has no exact “Burns” label. A narrow mapping combines “Burns (clinical),” “Burns (preclinical),” and “Burns (reviews),” totaling 93 records: 19 human reports, 67 animal publications, a standalone in-vitro assay plus one laboratory component overlapping a human report, five reviews or meta-analyses with overlap, and one protocol. They cover acute burns, skin-graft donor sites, grafts, and post-burn symptoms rather than one uniform indication. Some mapped records use modalities other than conventional PBM.

Human and clinical evidence

Small controlled studies report faster healing in selected settings. A double-blind pilot involving nine people with second-degree burns used red and near-infrared LED light; the investigators reported mean re-epithelialization in 7.56 days in treated areas versus 16 days in comparison areas. A randomized donor-site study involving 11 patients and 18 sites reported greater wound-size reduction after seven days with red light. A separate randomized trial in 24 people with second-degree burns found re-epithelialization in 8.3 versus 12.6 days when superpulsed near-infrared treatment was added to standard care; pain and wound-reduction measures also favored the light group, while inflammatory blood markers and microbial findings did not differ (Adler et al. 2025; Vaghardoost et al. 2018; Yadav et al. 2025). These are small studies of specific wounds and do not establish effects for every burn depth or long-term scar outcome.

Animal evidence

The mapped preclinical literature is largely rat experiments, with a smaller number of mouse studies. Many report changes in closure time, epithelialization, collagen organization, angiogenesis, or inflammatory measures; some are null or compare combined treatments such as light plus a dressing or cell therapy. The animal review and meta-analyses synthesize overlapping experiments rather than adding new animal cohorts.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Laboratory evidence is limited to a small number of assays, including one standalone assay and one laboratory component reported alongside a human study.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols include visible red light around 655–660 nm, red plus near-infrared 660/840 nm LEDs, and superpulsed 904 nm near-infrared laser. The 24-person trial used 10-minute sessions twice weekly at 1.1 J per session; the pilot used 2.4–7.7 J/cm² per session. Delivery, wound depth, comparator care, and schedule differ. The mapped category does not identify one optimal dose or device.

Interpretation

The strongest direct human findings concern short-term re-epithelialization or wound-size measures in selected second-degree burns and graft-donor sites. Those results support further testing of defined protocols. They should not be generalized to all burn types, and the literature provides less direct evidence about durable scar quality, function, or long-term safety.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for faster healing in selected second-degree and donor-site burns Low for pain, scarring, and long-term function
Publications and records93 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several small controlled human studies report faster re-epithelialization or donor-site closure with specific protocols, including a 24-person randomized trial. This supports a low-to-moderate rating for short-term healing in those settings, not for all burns. Protocols and wound types differ. Larger multicenter studies with standardized burn depth, healing measures, pain, scarring, and follow-up would strengthen broader conclusions.
